units.title: Complex Numbers and the Plane
units.blurb: Work with modulus, conjugate, exponential form and arguments, and describe regions of the plane.

units.title: Complex Functions
units.blurb: Split a complex function into real and imaginary parts, see it as a map of the plane, and take limits from every direction.

units.title: Analytic Functions
units.blurb: Differentiate in the complex sense, test with the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and meet harmonic functions.

units.title: Exponentials, Logarithms and Powers
units.blurb: Extend eˣ, sine, cosine, logarithms and powers to complex numbers, and handle the many values of log z with branches.

units.title: Contour Integrals and Cauchy's Theorem
units.blurb: Integrate along curves in the plane, then use Cauchy's theorem and integral formula and their consequences.

units.title: Power Series and Laurent Series
units.blurb: Expand analytic functions in power series on disks and Laurent series on annuli, and classify singularities.

units.title: Residues
units.blurb: Compute residues, use the residue theorem to evaluate real integrals, and count zeros with the argument principle.

units.title: Conformal Maps
units.blurb: Use analytic functions to map regions onto one another while keeping angles, with Möbius transformations as the main tool.

topics.title: Modulus and Conjugate
topics.short: |z|² = z·z̄ is a real number, |zw| = |z| |w|, and |z + w| ≤ |z| + |w|.
topics.trouble: Students treat z² and |z|² as the same thing. For z = 1 + i, z² = 2i, but |z|² = z·z̄ = 2.

topics.title: Euler's Formula and Exponential Form
topics.short: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, so z = re^(iθ); multiplying multiplies the lengths and adds the angles.
topics.trouble: Students find the angle with tan⁻¹(b/a) and land in the wrong quadrant: −1 − i has angle −3π/4 (or 5π/4), not π/4.

topics.title: Arguments and the Principal Argument
topics.short: arg z is a whole family of angles θ + 2πk; the principal value Arg z lies in (−π, π], and Arg(zw) can differ from Arg z + Arg w by 2π.
topics.trouble: Students assume Arg(zw) = Arg z + Arg w. For z = w = −1, Arg z + Arg w = 2π, but Arg(zw) = Arg 1 = 0.

topics.title: Curves and Regions in the Plane
topics.short: Read sets such as |z − 2i| < 3 (a disk), 1 < |z| < 2 (an annulus) and Re z > 0 (a half-plane), and tell open, closed, bounded and connected sets apart.
topics.trouble: Students read |z − 2i| < 3 as a disk centered at −2i. |z − a| is the distance from z to a, so the center is 2i.

topics.title: Complex Functions as u + iv
topics.short: Write f(z) = u(x, y) + i v(x, y): for f(z) = z², u = x² − y² and v = 2xy.
topics.trouble: Students keep the i inside v, writing v = 2ixy. The imaginary part v is the real-valued coefficient of i.

topics.title: Functions as Mappings
topics.short: Watch f move points from the z-plane to the w-plane: az + b rotates, scales and shifts, z² squares lengths and doubles angles, and 1/z turns the plane inside out.
topics.trouble: Students expect z² to send the first quadrant to itself. Doubling the angles sends it onto the upper half-plane.

topics.title: Limits and Continuity
topics.short: lim f(z) = L when f(z) approaches L along every path to z₀; z̄/z has no limit at 0.
topics.trouble: Students check only the real axis, or only straight lines, before declaring that a limit exists.

topics.title: The Complex Derivative
topics.short: f′(z₀) = lim (f(z₀ + h) − f(z₀))/h as h → 0 from every direction in the plane; z² is differentiable everywhere, and z̄ nowhere.
topics.trouble: Students assume a formula that is smooth in x and y, such as z̄ or |z|², must be complex differentiable.

topics.title: The Cauchy–Riemann Equations
topics.short: f = u + iv with continuous partial derivatives is differentiable exactly where uₓ = v_y and u_y = −vₓ, and there f′ = uₓ + i vₓ.
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign in u_y = −vₓ, or call a function analytic because the equations hold at a single point: |z|² is differentiable only at 0 and analytic nowhere.

topics.title: Analytic Functions
topics.short: f is analytic on an open set when it is differentiable at every point of it; sums, products, quotients and compositions follow the usual rules, and polynomials are entire.
topics.trouble: Students forget to remove the zeros of a denominator: (z + 1)/(z² + 1) is analytic everywhere except z = ±i.

topics.title: Harmonic Functions and Harmonic Conjugates
topics.short: The real and imaginary parts of an analytic function solve u_xx + u_yy = 0; given u, find v from the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
topics.trouble: Students integrate v_y = uₓ with respect to y and add a plain constant, when the "constant" can be any function of x; the other equation decides it.

topics.title: The Complex Exponential
topics.short: e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y): |e^z| = eˣ, e^z is never 0, and it repeats with period 2πi.
topics.trouble: Students expect e^z = w to have one solution. Adding any multiple of 2πi to a solution gives another.

topics.title: Complex Sine and Cosine
topics.short: cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2 and sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i) are entire and unbounded, so sin z = 2 has solutions.
topics.trouble: Students carry |sin z| ≤ 1 over from the real line, but |sin(iy)| = |sinh y| grows without bound.

topics.title: The Complex Logarithm
topics.short: log z = ln|z| + i arg z has infinitely many values, 2πi apart; the principal value is Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z.
topics.trouble: Students give log z a single value, or use Log(zw) = Log z + Log w, which can be off by 2πi: Log(−1) + Log(−1) = 2πi, but Log 1 = 0.

topics.title: Branches and Branch Cuts
topics.short: A branch chooses one value continuously on a cut plane: Log jumps by 2πi across its cut, the negative real axis, and a different cut gives a different branch.
topics.trouble: Students treat Log z as analytic everywhere except 0, though it is not even continuous on the negative real axis; or they think the cut belongs to log itself, when it is a choice.

topics.title: Complex Powers
topics.short: z^c = e^(c log z) can have many values: every value of i^i = e^(−π/2 − 2πk) is a real number.
topics.trouble: Students use real exponent rules such as (zw)^c = z^c w^c or (z^a)^b = z^(ab) with principal values, where they can fail.

topics.title: Contours and Parametrizations
topics.short: Describe segments and circles as z(t): z(t) = a + re^(it), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, goes once around the circle counterclockwise.
topics.trouble: Students use the counterclockwise formula for a clockwise path, which flips the sign of the integral.

topics.title: Contour Integrals
topics.short: ∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ f(z(t)) z′(t) dt; once around the unit circle, ∮ dz/z = 2πi.
topics.trouble: Students leave out the factor z′(t) and integrate f(z(t)) dt instead.

topics.title: Bounding Integrals: The ML Inequality
topics.short: |∫_C f(z) dz| ≤ M · L, where M bounds |f| on C and L is the length of C.
topics.trouble: Students bound 1/|z² + 1| on |z| = R with |z² + 1| ≤ R² + 1, which gives a lower bound for the fraction instead of an upper one. Use |z² + 1| ≥ R² − 1.

topics.title: Antiderivatives and Path Independence
topics.short: If F′ = f on an open set containing C, then ∫_C f dz = F(end) − F(start); 1/z has no antiderivative on any loop around 0.
topics.trouble: Students use Log z as an antiderivative of 1/z around a loop that circles 0 and get 0 instead of 2πi; Log is not analytic on its cut.

topics.title: Cauchy's Theorem
topics.short: If f is analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C, then ∮_C f(z) dz = 0.
topics.trouble: Students apply the theorem when a point where f is not analytic lies inside C.

topics.title: Deforming Contours
topics.short: An integral does not change when the contour slides across places where f is analytic, so ∮ dz/(z − a)ⁿ around a is 2πi for n = 1 and 0 for every other integer n.
topics.trouble: Students expect ∮ dz/(z − a)² to be 2πi like the case n = 1, but (z − a)⁻² has an antiderivative, so the integral is 0.

topics.title: Cauchy's Integral Formula
topics.short: If f is analytic on and inside C and a is inside C, then f(a) = (1/(2πi)) ∮_C f(z)/(z − a) dz.
topics.trouble: Students forget the factor 2πi, or use the formula when a lies outside C, where the integral is 0.

topics.title: Cauchy's Formula for Derivatives
topics.short: ∮_C f(z)/(z − a)^(n + 1) dz = 2πi f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n!, so an analytic function has derivatives of every order.
topics.trouble: Students take the power n + 1 as the order of the derivative, or leave out the n!.

topics.title: Liouville's Theorem and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
topics.short: A bounded entire function is constant, so every nonconstant polynomial has a complex root.
topics.trouble: Students offer sin z as a bounded entire function that breaks the theorem. It is bounded on the real line but not on the plane: |sin(iy)| = |sinh y|.

topics.title: The Maximum Modulus Principle
topics.short: On a bounded region, a nonconstant analytic function that is continuous up to the boundary reaches its largest |f| on the boundary, never inside.
topics.trouble: Students hunt for the maximum of |f| at a critical point inside the region, as with real functions of two variables.

topics.title: Power Series and Disks of Convergence
topics.short: Σ cₙ(z − a)ⁿ converges inside a disk and diverges outside it; find the radius with the ratio or root test.
topics.trouble: Students expect the Maclaurin series of 1/(1 + x²) to converge for every real x. Its radius is 1 because of the singularities at ±i.

topics.title: Taylor Series of Analytic Functions
topics.short: An analytic function equals its Taylor series on the largest open disk around a that avoids its singularities.
topics.trouble: Students reuse a known series without changing the center: about a = i, 1/(1 − z) needs powers of (z − i), and its radius is |1 − i| = √2.

topics.title: Laurent Series
topics.short: In an annulus, f = Σ cₙ(z − a)ⁿ with negative powers too: 1/(z(z − 1)) has one series on 0 < |z| < 1 and another on |z| > 1.
topics.trouble: Students expand 1/(z − 1) in powers of z where |z| > 1. There the geometric series must use powers of 1/z.

topics.title: Zeros and Isolated Singularities
topics.short: Classify an isolated singularity as removable, a pole of order m or essential, from the Laurent series or from limits.
topics.trouble: Students call (sin z)/z a pole at 0 (it is removable) or call e^(1/z) a pole (it is essential).

topics.title: Residues at Simple Poles
topics.short: The residue at a is the coefficient of 1/(z − a); at a simple pole it is lim (z − a) f(z), which is g(a)/h′(a) when f = g/h.
topics.trouble: Students use g(a)/h′(a) at a pole that is not simple, where the formula does not apply.

topics.title: Residues at Higher-Order Poles
topics.short: At a pole of order m, the residue is (1/(m − 1)!) times the limit of the (m − 1)st derivative of (z − a)ᵐ f(z).
topics.trouble: Students forget the factor 1/(m − 1)!, or use the wrong order m.

topics.title: The Residue Theorem
topics.short: ∮_C f(z) dz = 2πi times the sum of the residues of f at the poles inside C.
topics.trouble: Students include the residues at poles that lie outside the contour.

topics.title: Integrals over a Full Turn
topics.short: Turn ∫₀^{2π} R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ into a contour integral around the unit circle with z = e^(iθ), cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2 and dθ = dz/(iz).
topics.trouble: Students forget the factor dθ = dz/(iz), or count poles outside the unit circle.

topics.title: Improper Integrals with Residues
topics.short: Close the real line with a large half-circle in the upper half-plane; when deg Q ≥ deg P + 2, the arc adds nothing as the radius grows, so ∫ P/Q dx is 2πi times the upper residues.
topics.trouble: Students include the poles in the lower half-plane when closing the contour in the upper half.

topics.title: Integrals with Sines and Cosines
topics.short: For ∫ R(x) cos(ax) dx with a > 0, integrate R(z) e^(iaz) around the upper half-disk and take the real part.
topics.trouble: Students replace cos x by cos z, which grows without bound in the upper half-plane (cos(iy) = cosh y), instead of using e^(iz).

topics.title: The Argument Principle
topics.short: (1/(2πi)) ∮_C f′/f dz counts the zeros minus the poles inside C, which is the number of times f(C) winds around 0.
topics.trouble: Students count each zero once regardless of its multiplicity, or forget to subtract the poles.

topics.title: Rouché's Theorem
topics.short: If |g| < |f| everywhere on C, then f and f + g have the same number of zeros inside C.
topics.trouble: Students compare |g| and |f| at one point of C instead of all of it, or choose the wrong term as the larger one.

topics.title: Conformal Maps
topics.short: Where f is analytic and f′ ≠ 0, f keeps angles: tiny shapes are turned by arg f′ and scaled by |f′|.
topics.trouble: Students expect angles to be kept where f′ = 0, but z² doubles the angles at 0.

topics.title: Möbius Transformations
topics.short: w = (az + b)/(cz + d) with ad − bc ≠ 0 maps circles and lines to circles and lines, and, when c ≠ 0, sends −d/c to ∞ and ∞ to a/c.
topics.trouble: Students expect every circle to map to a circle, but a circle through −d/c maps to a line.

topics.title: A Möbius Map from Three Points
topics.short: Exactly one Möbius transformation sends three given points to three given points; find it with the cross-ratio.
topics.trouble: Students pair the points in the wrong order, which gives a different map.

topics.title: Mapping Standard Regions
topics.short: Send the upper half-plane to the unit disk with (z − i)/(z + i), open sectors with zⁿ and horizontal strips with e^z, and chain maps together.
topics.trouble: Students check where the boundary goes but not which side lands inside. Since (z − i)/(z + i) sends i to 0, the upper half-plane goes to the inside of the disk.
